analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum standards for health insurance and helps low-income and catastrophically ill people buy coverage.
analysis.headline: A 1989 bill to set minimum health insurance standards, require many employers to offer coverage, and fund help for low-income and catastrophically ill patients — introduced with 25 cosponsors, it never received a vote and died in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set federal minimum standards for health insurance plans — covering at least 80% of costs above a small deductible, capping yearly out-of-pocket spending at $3,000 per person, and requiring clear "qualified" or "nonqualified" labeling on every policy and ad. Employers with 10 or more workers would have to offer a certified plan that workers could keep or convert to individual coverage after leaving the job. Every state would have to run a comprehensive health insurance plan open to any resident, funded by insurer assessments, with federal grants to help low-income people buy coverage and to pay most costs for families hit by catastrophic illness.
analysis.who_benefits: People without health coverage or with thin coverage gain the most: guaranteed access to a state plan regardless of health status, out-of-pocket caps, and subsidies to buy coverage if they are low-income. Families facing catastrophic illness could have 90% or more of their expenses above an income-scaled threshold paid. Workers at employers with 10 or more employees would gain the right to portable coverage they can convert to an individual policy.

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 10 or more employees must offer a certified qualified plan that employees can continue for a year at group rates and then convert to individual coverage with no new underwriting restrictions, and that covers spouses and children.

Qualified plans must pay at least 80% of covered expenses above a deductible of no more than $250 per person, cap annual out-of-pocket costs at $3,000 per person ($6,000 per family), and carry a $1,000,000 lifetime maximum that insurers cannot substitute away.

Every state must establish a comprehensive health insurance plan open to all residents, as a condition of receiving Medicaid funds, with premiums initially pegged to the average rates of the state's five largest individual-plan insurers and later capped at 105% of state-employee group premiums.

The bill authorizes $2.47 billion a year in federal grants, matching 50% of state spending, to help low-income individuals purchase qualified coverage, and $575 million a year for a program paying at least 90% of catastrophic medical expenses above a threshold scaled to household income.

Every health policy and advertisement must be labeled "qualified" or "nonqualified," so buyers can tell whether a plan meets the minimum standards, with false labeling treated as an unfair practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 10 or more employees bear the cost of offering qualified coverage, facing civil penalties up to $10,000 for knowing noncompliance. Health insurers, HMOs, and self-insuring employers in each state must join a comprehensive health association, share the losses of the state plan, and have claims expenses assessed against them. Federal taxpayers fund the matching grants, and state taxpayers must cover at least 40% of the non-federal share.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate excludes new, part-time, part-year, young, bargaining-unit, and nonresident-alien employees from the definition of employee, and employers cannot be required to pay more than an existing collective-bargaining agreement or contract requires — leaving many lower-wage and contingent workers without the new protection.

Public assistance is routed through private insurers: each state's plan is administered by a selected "writing carrier" reimbursed for its direct and indirect expenses, and up to 12.5% of state-plan premiums can go to agent referral fees and carrier expenses rather than claims.
The insurer associations that run the state plans are exempt from federal and state antitrust laws, and association members and writing-carrier premiums are exempt from state taxation.

The federal support is modest and capped: each state's quarterly grant is limited to $2.50 per resident for low-income assistance and $0.625 per resident for catastrophic assistance, the money is authorized rather than guaranteed, and the catastrophic program only kicks in after a family has already absorbed expenses equal to 30-50% of income or $3,000 in a year.
Qualified plans may exclude for six months any condition diagnosed within 90 days before coverage began, so people who get sick just before enrolling can face a coverage gap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it reaches, the bill offers real, concrete protection: guaranteed-issue state coverage, out-of-pocket caps, and help with catastrophic bills. But it is an incremental design, not universal coverage — the employer mandate reaches only firms of 10 or more and carves out part-time and young workers, the federal money is small and capped per capita, and the state plans are built and administered by the insurance industry itself, complete with antitrust and tax exemptions and agent referral fees. A family buried under medical debt before hitting the eligibility threshold gets little. It is a genuine safety-net improvement wrapped around, and dependent on, the existing private insurance system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to three subcommittees, and it never came back — no hearing outcome, no markup, no floor vote, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Sabo introduced the bill on February 6, 1989, with six original cosponsors, and 25 members total signed on — 24 Democrats and one Republican.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced; no other committee action appears in the record.

On February 27, 1989, it was referred to three subcommittees — Health and the Environment; Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness; and Transportation and Hazardous Materials — and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill never received a vote in the House or the Senate, and no version of it became law before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers of 10 or more workers are better off, because the bill's mandates, loss-sharing assessments, and coverage requirements never took effect. The uninsured and low-income people the bill would have helped gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Martin Olav Sabo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 25 cosponsors for a minimum-standards, guaranteed-coverage health insurance proposal.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — never reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and referred it to three subcommittees; no markup, hearing outcome, or report ever appears in the record, and the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the House never recorded a position; sponsorship leaned Democratic (24 of the 25 cosponsors) with a single Republican, and whatever opposition kept the bill in subcommittee was never expressed on the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers, HMOs, and Blue Cross/Blue Shield plans
industries.note: The bill would have locked insurers into a permanent public role: every state's guaranteed-coverage plan would be run by a private "writing carrier" they select, with premium tax exemptions and an antitrust exemption for their associations. In exchange they would have to join mandatory associations, share the state plan's losses, accept open enrollment, and charge premiums capped relative to market rates.

They would have to offer certified, convertible, family-includable health coverage or face civil penalties up to $10,000, though the requirement exempts part-time, young, and bargaining-unit workers and is capped by existing contracts.
Every writing carrier would have to pay a referral fee to any agent who sends an accepted applicant to the state plan, funded from plan premiums up to the 12.5% administrative cap.
